planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Silver Sceptre produces narrow, arching blades edged in crisp silvery-white, keeping its brightest variegation where afternoon sun is filtered.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Silver Sceptre is a variegated selection of Japanese sedge, forming a tidy, fountain-like clump of fine, arching, dark-green leaves each edged in a crisp band of silvery white, brightening shaded borders and woodland edges without the maintenance a flowering perennial demands. It holds its evergreen foliage through mild winters and keeps its variegation strongest when protected from harsh midday sun, which can scorch or fade the white margins. Established clumps need only the occasional combing-out of tattered old leaves in early spring, and division every three to four years keeps plantings vigorous and prevents the center of the clump from thinning out.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

Royal Horticultural Society

common_name: Banana Boat Sedge (Golden Variegated Broadleaf Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist to consistently wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Banana Boat is a slow-creeping, rhizomatous broadleaf sedge with wide, bright yellow leaves that scorch quickly in direct sun.

directions: Plant in moist to consistently wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, avoiding direct sun which quickly scorches the bright foliage. Banana Boat is a broad-leaved sedge unlike the fine-bladed carex most gardeners picture, producing wide, softly arching, glowing yellow leaves with a thin green edge that lend a bold, almost tropical texture to deeply shaded beds under trees and along shaded stream banks. It spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing patch rather than a tight clump, filling gaps between hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials over two or three seasons. It tolerates periodically wet soil better than most sedges, making it a useful choice for shaded low spots, and needs little care beyond removing winter-damaged foliage in early spring.

common_name: Frosted Curls Carex (New Zealand Hair Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Frosted Curls forms a tousled mound of fine, curling, silvery pale-green foliage and tolerates shade well but is best kept out of deep, dense shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, though this New Zealand hair sedge also tolerates considerably more sun than most shade sedges provided moisture is adequate. Frosted Curls produces a loose, tumbling mound of very fine, hair-like leaves in a pale, frosted silvery-green that curls and twists at the tips, giving the whole clump a soft, textural, almost windswept look that pairs nicely with bolder-leaved shade perennials. It stays evergreen in mild climates and is useful at the front of a border, in containers, or cascading over a low wall where its curling texture can be seen up close. Comb out dead foliage in early spring and divide congested clumps every few years to keep the mound looking fresh; avoid deep, dense shade, which thins the plant and dulls its color.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
Royal Horticultural Society
North Carolina State Extension

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Everest carries crisp white-margined leaves year-round and colors best out of direct afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Everest is an evergreen Japanese sedge cultivar with narrow, gracefully arching leaves striped in bright white along the margins and deep green down the center, giving a crisp, frosty look that reads well from a distance in a shaded bed. It tolerates some gentle morning sun but colors up best and resists leaf scorch when protected from hot afternoon exposure, making it a dependable choice for the deeper, cooler shade under trees and on the north side of buildings. Deer generally leave it alone, and it needs little more than an early-spring grooming to remove tired winter foliage before new growth emerges. Its slowly spreading habit works well as a repeated accent along a shaded path or massed as a fine-textured groundcover.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
North Carolina State Extension
Royal Horticultural Society

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or fall; Berkeley sedge is a tough, drought-tolerant West Coast native forming a fine-textured, fountain-like clump widely used as a lawn substitute or border edging in shaded gardens.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, though established plants also tolerate considerably more sun in cooler coastal climates. Berkeley sedge forms a dense, evergreen, fountain-shaped clump of narrow, glossy dark-green blades that arch gracefully outward, making it one of the more durable shade sedges for dry, root-competitive spots under trees where turf and thirstier groundcovers struggle. It is notably drought tolerant once established and needs only occasional deep watering through the dry season, along with a yearly shearing or combing-out of old foliage in late winter to keep clumps looking fresh. Its fine, uniform texture and slowly clumping (not aggressively spreading) habit make it a popular substitute for turfgrass in shaded areas, along woodland paths, and as edging beneath trees and shrubs.

common_name: Lake Emerald Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Florida Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil, spacing vines a bit wider than most bunch grapes to accommodate its vigor; Lake Emerald is a light-green, Pierce's disease-resistant Florida bunch grape developed by the University of Florida for wine and juice production.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing extra space between vines since Lake Emerald is a vigorous grower recommended for wider row spacing than most other Florida bunch grapes. Developed by the University of Florida's bunch grape breeding program at Leesburg, it is prized for strong resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by leafhoppers that has historically limited grape growing across the humid Gulf South, and it does not require grafting onto a resistant rootstock except in soils with a naturally high pH. It produces light green, juicy berries used mainly for wine and juice or jelly rather than fresh eating, ripening in midsummer just after the purple 'Blue Lake' cultivar. As with other Florida bunch grapes, a preventive fungicide spray program through the growing season is important to control the fungal fruit rots that thrive in hot, humid weather, and vines should be pruned hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Bunch Grape (HS17A)

common_name: Orlando Seedless Grape (First Pierce's Disease-Resistant Seedless Bunch Grape)

planting.note: Plant vines grafted onto 'Tampa' or 'Dog Ridge' rootstock in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Orlando Seedless was the first seedless bunch grape combining Pierce's disease resistance, released from the University of Florida's Leesburg breeding program.

directions: Plant grafted vines in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, since Orlando Seedless requires grafting onto 'Tampa' or 'Dog Ridge' rootstock for satisfactory growth and yield rather than growing on its own roots. Bred from interspecific crosses at the University of Florida's Agricultural Research Center in Leesburg, it was the first bunch grape to pair genuine seedlessness with resistance to Pierce's disease, the leafhopper-spread bacterial infection that devastated Florida's historic bunch grape industry. Its white, seedless fruit has good eating quality and fresh-market appeal, though the variety is notably more susceptible to anthracnose than other Florida-bred cultivars and can suffer berry shattering as clusters mature, so a consistent fungicide spray program from bud break onward is important. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to reduce disease pressure and improve berry size.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Bunch Grape (HS17A)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bunch Grape Cultivars for Florida
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Grape Variety Selection for Pierce's Disease Areas

common_name: Daytona Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Pink Dooryard Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Daytona, released by the University of Florida in the early 1980s, is a pink-fruited bunch grape bred for home dooryard use with strong tolerance to Pierce's disease and downy mildew.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy. Daytona was released in the early 1980s from the University of Florida's bunch grape breeding program and is grown chiefly as a home dooryard grape, valued for its pink-blushed fruit and for standing up to Pierce's disease and downy mildew far better than European wine grapes in Florida's hot, humid climate. It does remain somewhat susceptible to anthracnose, ripe rot, black rot, and powdery mildew, so an ongoing fungicide program through the growing season is worthwhile even on a resistant cultivar like this one. Fruit is best suited to fresh eating off the vine rather than commercial wine or juice production. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and reduce disease pressure in humid weather.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Bunch Grape (HS17A)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bunch Grape Cultivars for Florida

common_name: Blue Lake Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Purple Dooryard Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Blue Lake is a purple-fruited, Pierce's disease-resistant Florida bunch grape used for dooryard eating and juice or jelly, growing well on its own roots in most soils.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing good airflow through the canopy. Blue Lake is a purple Florida bunch grape carrying strong resistance to Pierce's disease, one of a small group of University of Florida-recommended cultivars able to shrug off the bacterial infection that limits most European wine grapes across the humid Gulf South. Unlike several of its Florida-bred counterparts, it typically grows well on its own roots and does not need grafting onto a resistant rootstock except in alkaline soils, simplifying establishment for home growers. Its purple berries are used both for fresh dooryard eating and for juice and jelly making, ripening in midsummer shortly after the earlier 'Stover' cultivar. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and maintain a preventive fungicide program to control the fungal fruit rots that are the main remaining disease threat in Florida's hot, humid summers.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Bunch Grape (HS17A)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Grape Variety Selection for Pierce's Disease Areas

common_name: MidSouth Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Mississippi Bunch Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; MidSouth, released by Mississippi State University in 1981 from decades-old USDA breeding work in Meridian, Mississippi, is a self-fertile, highly Pierce's disease-tolerant bunch grape long grown across the Deep South mainly for jelly and juice.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the moderately vigorous canopy. MidSouth was released by Mississippi State University in 1981, tracing back to USDA breeding work begun in the late 1930s at the Meridian, Mississippi field station, and it remains valued today for its exceptional tolerance of Pierce's disease across Mississippi, Louisiana, and neighboring Gulf South states. Its self-fertile vines produce clusters of dark blue-purple berries covered in a heavy waxy bloom that ripen in late July to mid-August in the southern part of its range, with a rich, sweet-tart flavor carrying a hint of raspberry; the seeded, slip-skin berries are best suited to jelly and juice rather than fresh table use. The vine is more susceptible to fungal disease and root-knot nematodes than to Pierce's disease itself, so a regular fungicide program and nematode-aware site selection help keep plantings productive. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons to keep cluster and berry size from declining.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Fruit and Nut Review: Bunch Grapes
Mississippi State University Scholars Junction — Reintroducing a Multiuse Bunch Grape for the Deep South: 'MidSouth'
